newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech funds penalties may herald clean-up campaign.
newsitem.headline: Czech funds penalties may herald clean-up campaign.

text.p: Tough penalties imposed on two big Czech bank-owned fund managers may herald a new campaign to clean up financial markets and restore investor confidence after a series of scandals, analysts said on Thursday.

The finance ministry said it had fined investment fund manager Prvni Investicni a.s. (PIAS), a unit of bank IPB, the maximum permissible 10 million crowns ($308,000) for illegal financing operations and other violations.

The ministry said on Tuesday that its securities overseeing bureau would impose forced administration on investment company OB Invest (OBI), part of the Ceskoslovesnsko Obchodni Banka a.s. (CSOB) finance and business group, because of repeated violations of financial laws.

"With this current wave of fining and investigation, I think the finance ministry is finally showing its teeth and that it means to clean up this sector, which needs a lot of cleaning," said Eric Volkman, equity analyst specialising in funds at Raiffeisen Capital and Investment in Prague.
"There have been fines before but they have been fairly small and, more to the point, they have been kept secret."

Investors have complained for years about a lack of regulation and transparency in Czech financial markets and analysts have cited this as one reason why Czech stocks have lagged shares in Warsaw and Budapest, for example.

In response to growing public disquiet over economic crime, which was one reason for a fall in the popularity of the government, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus ordered steps in April to tighten market regulation.
"It has been clear that things could not continue in the way they were and the finance ministry realised that they had to do something," said Jan Sykora of Wood & Company.
One aim of the steps, unveiled in the first of two recent economic revitalisation packages, is to improve relations between the largely state-owned banks and the investment funds.
Analysts say the fact that the funds own large stakes in many Czech companies, snapped up after voucher privatisation in 1992-95, is a major brake on essential restructuring.
"Practically, you can say they haven't really privatised," said Sykora. "The companies where the funds are significant holders tend to underperform their peers in the industry," he added.
As part of its package, the government acknowledged the need to set up an independent securities committee.
Prague Stock Exchange chairman Tomas Jezek said this week parliament's budget committee on September 24 would discuss the draft law setting up the commission.
Jezek said he was confident the new body would have teeth and that efforts to weaken it would be reversed.
"The worst thing is that the government has dropped many (enforcement) powers...I have discussed this with many deputies and I am sure that they will correct this."

The tougher stance against securities law violations follows a period of aggressive speculative selling of the crown by investors dismayed at growing political instability and a worsening economic situation.
The central bank eventually floated the crown in late May.
